body: The papers went into Hale’s pigeonhole at nine this morning. Lena’s was in it already, squared at the corners under a black binder clip, looking like it had been there since the building opened. At five past nine, from the Hollis steps, Jack called Greyhound and told a woman in customer service he’d had a better offer, exactly as instructed. She didn’t ask from whom. The voucher is in the mail.
At one o’clock, the board at the front of 302 hasn’t been erased since Wednesday. The question is still up there in Hale’s capitals, and so are the two of them, by name:

body.title: Hollis 302 whiteboard
body.text:
WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE.
(MR. COSTIGAN: NO. MISS BROUSSARD: YES. PROVE THE THING YOU LEAST BELIEVE.)

body: Hale comes in at eight minutes past with the stack under one arm and a coffee from somewhere better than the Commons, and he doesn’t sit. He deals the papers down the long table, each pair’s swapped across, and Lena’s eight pages slide to a stop in front of Jack. His go two seats down, to her.

“Margins by tomorrow,” Hale says. “In ink, and in the margin, which is what a margin is for. Then slide them under each other’s doors, like Victorians. I’ll collect them in December, when I’ve recovered.”
He looks down the table over the coffee. “Which of you is staying in Marisol for the holiday?”
Not one hand goes up. At the far end Yusuf says, “Fremont. My mother’s doing a turkey and a biryani. The turkey is load-bearing for my father. It goes back in the refrigerator untouched.”
“Excellent,” says Hale, and seems to mean it. “I shall have the town to myself.”

Then he gives them fifty minutes on Hume, who would have disliked every one of them, and at ten to two he looks at the clock and lets them go. “Go home. Eat something that had a mother. Try not to convert anyone over the gravy.”
On the way out Lena holds Jack’s paper up by one corner. “Eight pages of you not believing something,” she says, in what the cold has left her. “I’m going to enjoy this.”

s09.slug: MONDAY · 2:10 PM · HOLLIS STEPS → DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL
body: The Hollis steps face south and keep the sun, and by ten past two half the seminar is sitting on them in it, not ready to go anywhere. Lena has the step below his with her knees up and his paper open across them, a red pen already working, making small noises of outrage on page two. Jack has hers. He hasn’t gotten past her first paragraph, because she’s right in it, and he is sitting in the sun being annoyed about that.
The RAZR has been off since one. He turns it on, and it buzzes in his hand before the screen has finished saying hello.

body: On the step below, Lena looks up from page two. Whatever she sees on him, she caps the pen.

She doesn’t ask. She reaches up and takes her paper out of his hand, which has started to crush it, folds it once and pushes it into the inside pocket of the Carhartt, flat against his chest. Then she holds up his. “Call her,” she says. “I’ll keep yours warm.”

He doesn’t call from the steps. The signal on the steps comes and goes, and he isn’t going to lose his mother to it. He walks to Delgado, and then he runs, and he takes the east stairs two at a time to the fourth-floor landing, where it holds. He gets most of a Hail Mary said between two and four. He dials with his back to the cinderblock.

It’s quarter past five on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up before the first ring has finished, from the kitchen, and she has gone calm, the way she does in hospitals. He can hear the nylon of her coat every time she moves the phone.

“She’s okay. Listen to me first. She’s okay.” Then the rest, in order, the way she’d give it to the school nurse. Nonna went up the stairs this afternoon — the stairs she has been sleeping in the front-room chair for a week to keep off — because she wanted her good rosary from the dresser, the one from San Giovanni. She had decided God could tell the difference. She got the rosary. She came down the fast way.

He knows those stairs. Fourteen of them, steep, under the brown runner Nonna picked out herself, with the seventh tread that complains no matter where you step on it; he carried her laundry up them from the time he was ten so she wouldn’t have to.
Gina found her at the bottom when she got in from Ursuline, and called the ambulance, and went out to the garage for her father.

“Gina did everything right,” his mother says. “Fifteen years old, and she did every single thing right, Jack — the towel, the ambulance, my number, your father — and now she’s up in her room with the door shut and she won’t come down. Text her later. Not now. Later.”

“A broken wrist. Six stitches over the eye. And they’re keeping her at St. Elizabeth’s for her heart — a monitor, for the dizzy spells. They want to see what it does at night. She’s *stable*, that’s their word.” A breath. “She told the paramedic he was handsome. Then she wouldn’t get in his ambulance. She said she’d go with Frank.” Another breath, and something that might be a laugh if it were any other day. “And I’m to tell Giacomino it wasn’t the stairs. She was in a hurry, and the rosary wasn’t.”
“Pop drove her?”
“Your father drove her. He was sober, Jack. I want you to know that. He carried her out to the truck himself.”

body.text: Somebody picks up the extension in the front hall. “She asked for you,” his father says. “Then she asked about the Browns.” “Thirty-seven points, Pop.” “And we lose.” Click.

body: “I can get a bus tonight. The paper’s in.”

“You will not. Wednesday is soon enough.” A cupboard; the clink of a pill bottle going into a bag. “You’ve got your paper.” “I turned it in, Ma.” “Then you’ve got another one. You always have another one. She’d get up out of that bed and kill you.”
“And Theo’s still coming?”
“Wednesday. He bought plane tickets.”
“*Plane* tickets.” She takes a moment over the price of them. “Madonna. Does he eat? Your father says he’s all bones and a wristwatch.”
“He eats, Ma.”
“He’ll eat here.”

body.text: “And your friend? The girl. Lena.” “She’s going home, Ma. New Orleans.” “Of course she is. Her mother’d want her.”

body: Then, because the list in her head has a next thing on it: “You know what she asked me, with the stitches in? First thing? Is the cow girl still coming at Christmas. She wants to make her the pizzelle. With a broken wrist, Jack, she’s planning *pizzelle*.”

response: “Ma.” He stops her at the pizzelle. “Becca and me — it’s done. Last Wednesday. It was me. I did it.”
“Oh, honey,” his mother says.

And then the line is quiet all the way to Glenwood Avenue, and Jack sits on the cold step and listens to it. Somewhere behind her a cupboard closes. Rosie asks something, far off, and is answered in a whisper.
When she comes back she’s brisk again. “I’ll write her anyway.”
“Ma —”

“She wrote Rosie on her birthday, Jack. I can write her at Christmas.” Something zips: the bag, on the table, with the rosary from San Giovanni on top where Nonna will see it first. “I have to get back up there before they give her the green Jell-O. She hates the green.” Then she’s gone, to St. Elizabeth’s, in the coat she never took off.
He stays on the landing step with the phone shut in his hand and Lena’s eight pages folded against his chest, where she put them. It’s twenty-five past two. In Youngstown it’s already dark.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound. Theo’s coming. I asked him at halftime of Michigan; he said yes before I finished. Two seats to Pittsburgh, Wednesday. The Greyhound’s a voucher. Monday Nonna fell. I told Ma about Becca on the same call. Theo and I fly Wednesday — my first time up.

body.text: Praying. Mémère too. I have your paper. —L.

body: By a quarter past six it’s dark, and the mailroom is a wall of little brass doors under one tube that hums.

body.text: His has an envelope in it with a return address he could read with his eyes shut, TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION in block capitals across the corner.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
PROFESSOR,
She said hey back. She said it like she meant it. You know what that means right. RIGHT?
Jagoff was mine first. You can keep it. Merry Christmas early.
Ma says Idaho’s coming at Christmas. The cow stationery one. Be nice to her. Don’t do the thing where you get funny.
Push-ups 160.
—D.
Advice for two weeks that are over, mailed a week ago from a place where the news comes on visiting Sundays. He reads it standing at the boxes, and puts it in the Carhartt with the other four.

body: Theo is at his desk in 412 in the navy robe with the MacBook open. Jack told him at three, from the doorway, short, and Theo said “Okay,” and got up and poured him a glass of the San Pellegrino he doesn’t share.
Now he turns the laptop around. A brick hospital in better weather than Youngstown has ever had: ST. ELIZABETH HEALTH CENTER, and under it, in a box, the hours.
“Two to eight,” Theo says. “We land in Pittsburgh at — it doesn’t matter. We’ll make it. I’m bringing her something.” He uncaps a pen. “What do Calabrian grandmothers like?”
“Being right.”
“I can bring that,” Theo says, and writes something on the back of his hand, under the place where *Glenwood* hasn’t quite washed off.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked.

Priya is working her way along the doors with a clipboard and a laminated card that says BREAK CLOSURE CHECKLIST, and as he passes she reads him his own without looking up: “Window locked, fridge unplugged, no perishables, Costigan. That includes the cheese. I know about the cheese.”
In the empty lounge the morning comes flat through the windows onto Margot’s whiteboard.

body: He stands in the doorway long enough to be late for Laney.

Laney has three suitcases, monogrammed, and a hatbox. “What’s in the hatbox?” “A *hat*, Jack.” She takes it from him on the stairs and carries it herself. They go down to the Anacapa lot in two trips. At the curb a black town car idles with a driver in a cap who doesn’t get out, and from the phone on the driver’s dash a woman with forty years of Texas in her voice is already talking.
“Delaney Rose. Shoulders. Somebody could be taking your picture.”
“Mama, it’s a *parking lot*.”
“That’s where they get you, baby.”
Laney puts her shoulders back. “Bye, Mama. I’m hanging you up now.” “You are not hanging up on your own m—” The driver, who has clearly done this before, reaches over and takes care of it.

Then she turns around and hugs Jack — fast and hard, sunglasses and all, a thing she does about once a semester — and says into his collar, “Eat. Sleep. And don’t learn any girls’ names, sugar. You’re fragile.” She lets go while he’s still finding his face, and gets into the town car, and four floors up, in the window of 412, Theo in the navy robe lifts one hand to her like an admiral in reduced circumstances.
Lena has a nine-thirty she won’t skip, cold or no cold; she and Laney said goodbye at seven, at length, according to Laney.

The town car goes. Margot is on the curb with a black duffel and a yellow paperback, riding with Kevin as far as San Jose and flying out from there. “Portland,” she says. “Two academics and a Tofurky. The annual seminar.” She looks at Jack with the interest she usually keeps for footnotes, and says nothing whatsoever about telephones.

body: “Today’s the Vietnamese Martyrs,” he says, wedging. “A hundred and seventeen of them. At La Vang they read every name at the evening Mass, and the readers split them up, and my mom reads eleven. She’s been practicing since October. She calls me to check her tones and then tells me mine are wrong.” He shuts the hatch. “They are. Then Thursday my dad fries a turkey in a fryer he bought at Costco in 2004 and has been afraid of every year since, and my sister stands by with the extinguisher. It’s a tradition.”
Then he straightens up and looks at Jack in the clean morning light, and the look goes where a pre-med’s look goes, to the eyebrow.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “whoever closed that was in a hurry.”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar.

body: Under the gargle of the Hobart, Rudy’s transistor has KNX on low, and between the traffic and the weather the business report says Koenigsegg has walked away from buying Saab. General Motors is disappointed, KNX says, and will be assessing its options.
“Poor Swede,” says Rudy, working the scraper down the flat-top in long strokes toward the trough.
At the counter Merle looks up from his chowder. “Brother-in-law had a Saab,” he says. “Started every morning like it was doing him a favor.” He goes back to the chowder.

Jack, at the sink, thinks of a red car sunned pink with a dent in the door and one taillight. In the garage on Glenwood his father will have heard it on the radio this morning and had one opinion about it, and Jack could tell you which. He racks the cups.

It’s the last shift before the break, and the Tuesday crowd is two fishermen at the counter and a couple in the back booth splitting a patty melt down the middle. Jack told Gloria about Nonna at seven, at the time clock, because she asked what was wrong with his face. She went into the walk-in for longer than the walk-in takes. At twenty to ten she is at the register with a white pie box and the spool of red-and-white string, and in the box is a pie, all of it, the top gone dark and glossy and studded edge to edge.
“Pecan,” Gloria says. “Pecan travels.” She runs the string around twice and ties it off with one pull. “Tell her it’s from a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. She’ll know what it means.”
“How old?”
“Eighty-four.”
“And she broke it going *up*?”
“For her rosary.”
Gloria thinks about that and seems satisfied with it. “Then she had a reason. You fall for a reason, it doesn’t count against you.”

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August.
